To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the pro-inflammatory cytokine/chemokine response of endocervix derived polarized epithelial cells to C. tracchomatis infection is modest and delayed, but that the constitutive T cell chemokinse response is significantly reduced.

the endocervical mucosa, the site of Chlamydia infections in the female reproductive tract, does not produce a robust pro-inflammatory response to chlamydial challenge, and this is due to the ability of chlamydia to evade host immune responses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the host immune response of endocervix derived epithelial cells to Chlamydia infection.
the role of the epithelium in the host response to C. tracohmatitis.
the host-pathogen interaction of Chlamydia in the endocervical mucosa, and how these bacteria evade the host response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Chlamydia infection of the endocerical epithelium results in a modest cytokine response, and a decrease in constitutive secretion of chemokines that recruit T cells to the endocervical mucosa.
C. tracomatis does not induce a robust inflammatory cytokine and chemokinetic response in endocervical cells, and may in fact dampen the response.

C. tracchomatis infection of endocervix epithelial cells induces only a modest pro-inflammatory response, and a decrease in chemokine secretion, and that the infection is not cleared by this response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

Chlamydiae can evade a robust pro-inflammatory immune response from endocervical cells by decreasing T cell chemoattractant secretion and by inducing anti-inflammatory cytokine secretion, which may allow them to establish and sustain infection in vivo.

the epithelial cells of the endocvix are not a major source of pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion during chlamydial infection, and that C. trahomatis may have developed strategies to evade a pro-inflammatory cytokine/chemokine response.
C. tracahomatis infection of endocervix derived epithelial cells results in a modest cytokine response and an inhibition of T cell chemotactic chemokines.
The main takeaway from our work is that
C. tracohmatis infection results in modest pro-inflammatory cytokines responses in endocervical cells, which are likely insufficient to clear chlamydia infection.
Chlamydia infection does not induce a robust pro-inflammatory response in endocervical cells, but does induce a decrease in T-cell chemokine secretion.
the epithelium is not as responsive as we thought it was.
